problem_statement: The paper frames multiasset derivative pricing as an important financial engineering task, especially when the derivative payoff is complex and must be computed numerically. It focuses on pricing derivatives by solving the Black–Scholes PDE for the present price of the derivative.
problem_statement_quotes: Pricing a multiasset derivative is an important problem in financial engineering, both theoretically and practically.

For such a simple derivative, the theoretical price can be computed analytically in some models, such as the Black–Scholes (BS) model [27]. If one wishes to calculate prices for derivatives with more complex payoffs, numerical calculations are required [28].

The goal of derivative pricing is to find the present price of the derivative, that is, V (0, s0), where s0 = (s1,0, . . . , sd,0)⊤∈Rd

is the present price of the underlying assets. To this end, we use the BSPDE, which describes the time evolution of V (t, s) [29], [30].
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical finite difference methods for the Black–Scholes PDE as the main baseline, and also references classical numerical ODE solvers after discretization. It contrasts its approach with classical FDM-based pricing of multiasset derivatives.
classical_baseline_quotes: Although it is suitable to numerically solve partial differential equations to calculate the prices of certain types of derivatives, the computational complexity increases exponentially as the number of underlying assets increases in some classical methods, such as the finite difference method.

Consider solving (3) using the FDM. In the FDM, we discretize the PDE with respect to the underlying asset prices and obtain the ODE. Then, we can use a numerical solver for ODEs, such as the Euler method and Runge–Kutta method [49].
This means that their method has substantial speedup compared with the classical FDM.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical finite-difference approach becomes exponentially expensive as the number of underlying assets grows, because the grid size scales as the product of per-asset grid points. It also states that achieving error level ϵ requires ngr proportional to ϵ−1/2, leading to time and space complexity O((1/ϵ)O(d)).
classical_difficulty_quotes: However, in the case of multiasset derivatives, the number of grid points increases exponentially with respect to the number of referenced assets, making price calculation difficult.
If we take ngr in proportion to ϵ−1/2 to achieve the error level ϵ (see Lemma II.1 in [31]), classical FDM requires the computational complexity of O((1/ϵ)O(d)) in terms of time and space.1,2
Then, the dimension of ¯V(τ ) is O((1/ϵ)d/2). Thus, it becomes difficult to solve the BSPDE discretized by FDM using the classical algorithm when multiple assets need to be considered.
extraction_notes: Clear motivation in abstract and introduction; paper is focused on derivative pricing and classical FDM scaling limits.
